profile.name: Sinte Gleska University Cultural Context
profile.tagline: Tribal land-grant university context and Northern Plains cultural preservation
profile.insight: Sinte Gleska University, named after Brulé Lakota chief Sinte Gleska, established an annual Northern Plains Indian Art Market incorporating dance and music education.
profile.profile: Sinte Gleska University is a public tribal land-grant university located in Mission, South Dakota, on the Rosebud Indian Reservation. Chartered by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe in 1970, the institution promotes and preserves the traditional Lakol Wicohan way of life. The university previously hosted the Northern Plains Indian Art Market, which featured juried art shows, powwows, and education in Northern Plains dance and music. Provided sources document this tribal educational institution rather than the West African Guinean dance tradition of the same name.
profile.profile_long: Sinte Gleska University operates as a public tribal land-grant institution situated in Mission, South Dakota, directly on the Rosebud Indian Reservation. The campus serves the Sicangu, or Burnt Thigh people of the Brulé Lakota Indian Reservation, with an enrollment of 828 full and part-time students. Regional accreditation is maintained through the Higher Learning Commission. The establishment of the college originated from a charter granted by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe in 1970, leading to the commencement of classes on February 3, 1971. Naming honors the Brulé Lakota chief Sinte Gleska. Leadership at inception included founding Board President and Lakota elder Stanley Red Bird Sr., alongside Joseph M. Marshall III, recognized as the first published writer in Lakota. In 1994, federal designation established it as a land-grant college alongside thirty-one other tribal institutions. Educational philosophy at the institution centers on promoting and preserving the Lakol Wicohan traditional way of life for future generations. Academic offerings span associate degrees, bachelor's degrees, master's degrees, certificates, and vocational programs across seven undergraduate departments: Arts and Sciences, Business, Education, Human Services, Lakota Studies, the Great Plains Art Institute, and the Institute of Technologies. Programs encompass Lakota language, aesthetics, and specialized graduate partnerships, such as a master's degree in education with an emphasis in early childhood special education offered in conjunction with Red Crow Community College and Old Sun Community College in Alberta, Canada. In 1988, the institution established the annual Northern Plains Indian Art Market in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. This event incorporated a juried art show, art market, powwow, and the Oscar Howe lecture, designed specifically to educate students and the community regarding Northern Plains art, philosophy, dance, and music. Financial challenges and decreasing student participation ultimately led to the cancellation of the market in 2023. Notable faculty members associated with the institution across its history include LeAnne Howe of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, Joe L. Kincheloe, Simon J. Ortiz of Acoma Pueblo, Albert White Hat, and Doris Leader Charge. While external catalogue records link the term 'Sinte' to a coastal Guinean pre-initiation dance and rhythm, the sources materials exclusively document the history, academic programs, and cultural preservation efforts of Sinte Gleska University in South Dakota.

sections.origins_and_history: Sinte Gleska University was charted by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe in 1970 and held its first classes on February 3, 1971, in Mission, South Dakota. The institution was named for the Brulé Lakota chief Sinte Gleska, with founding leadership including Lakota elder Stanley Red Bird Sr. and Joseph M. Marshall III. In 1994, it received land-grant college designation alongside 31 other tribal colleges.
